title: ‘Mind-reading’ AI tool can see what you see
source_used: New York Post (The Times page not in fulltext folder; NY Post carries the same story)
key_facts: Israeli scientists built a system called Brain-IT that reconstructs images people are viewing from their fMRI brain scans.
The work, led by Michal Irani of the Weizmann Institute of Science, is described in a paper submitted to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
It was trained on over 70,000 images collected while eight subjects viewed pictures.
A back-and-forth step (image to predicted scan to image) lets the models build themselves a large synthetic training set.
Irani says it works with about one hour of scanning for a new subject, rather than many hours for earlier methods.
The system identified 128 functional brain regions shared across people.
Irani suggests uses in helping paralysed people communicate; neuroscientist Tommy Sprague (UC Santa Barbara) says covert reading of thoughts would be worrying.
quote_evidence: produces reconstructions that more closely resemble the viewed images both structurally and semantically
None of us can afford 40 hours of imaging for a new subject
150 years of sci-fi can come true anytime, and that’s worrisome in a lot of ways
why_it_matters_hint: Cheaper brain decoding could help communication for paralysed people but raises privacy questions.
notes: Pool item was The Times (unreadable here); read the New York Post's version instead. Paper only submitted to ICLR, not yet peer-reviewed as far as the article says. The NY Post piece is tabloid in tone; claims about accuracy are the researchers'.
